title: TypeScript structural types versus C# nominal types
hook: TypeScript checks shape, not names — if two types have the same properties, they are compatible. C# is nominal: class names and inheritance hierarchies determine assignability even when shapes match.

blocks.text: **Structural typing** (TypeScript, Go interfaces) means compatibility is based on **members present** — `interface Point { x: number; y: number }` matches any object with those fields. **Nominal typing** (C#, Java) requires explicit inheritance or implementation: `class A` is not assignable to `class B` even with identical fields unless `A : B`. TypeScript's model enables duck typing at compile time but erases at run time — no runtime type tags. C# CLR enforces nominal types at run time via casting and reflection.

entries.plainDefinition: Types compatible if shapes match — names do not matter.
entries.example: { id: string } assignable to interface User { id: string }

entries.plainDefinition: Types compatible only through declared relationship.
entries.example: C# class Dog cannot substitute class Cat

entries.plainDefinition: Object literals cannot have extra properties not in target type.
entries.example: { id: "1", hack: true } rejected for User

entries.plainDefinition: TS types vanish at emit — structural rules are compile-time only.

blocks.text: C# developers new to TypeScript expect `implements` to create a nominal bond — it does not at run time. Accidental structural matches let unrelated types flow through APIs. **Branded types** and **discriminated unions** restore domain safety. Interviewers ask: 'Can two unrelated interfaces be assignable?' (Yes, if shapes match.) 'Does implements enforce at runtime?' (No.)

blocks.title: implements is compile-time only
blocks.body: class Foo implements Bar {} checks Foo has Bar's members — no CLR-style interface table at runtime.

blocks.title: Mental model for C# → TS migration

items.title: Same shape = compatible
items.body: Unrelated interfaces with matching fields are interchangeable to the checker.

items.title: Excess props on literals only
items.body: Variable assignment is bivariant on extra props; object literals are strict.

items.title: Use tags for domain safety
items.body: Discriminated unions with kind field — like C# sum types with pattern matching.

items.title: Branded types for IDs
items.body: type UserId = string & { __brand: 'UserId' } — nominal flavor at compile time.

blocks.title: Type system philosophy
rows: Interfaces at compile, nominal at runtime

blocks.title: Expecting nominal safety by default
blocks.body: Use discriminated unions, brands, or validation — structural typing will not stop wrong-shaped objects from variables.

blocks.text: TypeScript's structural rules have edge cases: function parameter types are checked bivariantly in some legacy positions (strictFunctionTypes fixes callbacks). Intersection types combine members — conflicts become never. Freshness (excess property) applies to object literals and some union assignments. For API boundaries, treat external data as unknown — structural assignability does not validate JSON shape.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected
blocks.body: Saying TypeScript is object-oriented like C#. Claiming implements creates runtime checks. Not knowing excess property rules apply to literals only.

interviewTakeaways: implements and interface are compile-time only — erased at emit.
Excess property checks apply to object literals, not all assignments.
60s: TS structural — same members = compatible. C# nominal — need inheritance. Use tagged unions and brands when you need domain separation. No runtime type tags in TS.
Follow-up: how do branded types work?
commonPitfalls: Weak: TS classes are nominal like C# — they are still structural for interface matching.
Weak: implements enforces at runtime — it does not.
Strong: Structural at compile, erased at runtime. Discriminated unions and brands for safety. C# CLR keeps nominal identity.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS has always been structural — if it walks like a duck... TypeScript formalizes that at compile time.
Branded types and discriminated unions add C#-like domain separation without CLR nominal enforcement.
